Question
========
`a <- 1:6` and `b <- 1:2` are two vectors. When you run `a + b`, R recycles the elements of `b` without printing a
warning. Why doesn't R warn you in this case?

Answerlist
----------
* Because the length of `a` (6) is evenly divisible by the length of `b` (2), so every element of `b` gets used the
  same number of times, with nothing left over.
* Because `a` and `b` are both integer vectors.
* Because R only warns about recycling when the shorter vector has exactly one element.
* Because addition never triggers recycling warnings, unlike other arithmetic operators.
* Because `b` was created using `:` instead of `c()`.

Solution
========
R only warns about recycling when the shorter vector's length does *not* evenly divide the longer vector's length.
In those cases, at least one "leftover" element gets used a different number of times than the rest, which is often a
sign of a mistake. When the shorter length divides the longer one evenly (as with lengths 6 and 2 here), every
element of the shorter vector is reused the same number of times, so R treats it as intentional and stays silent.
